details:
**Lake Baikal**
The world's deepest and oldest lake, in southern Siberia, divided into three basins by underwater ridges. It is home to the nerpa, an endemic freshwater seal. The Buryat Republic lies along its eastern shore, and the Angara River is its only outflow.

**Ural Mountains**
The mountain range usually treated as Siberia's western boundary, and as the dividing line between European and Asian Russia. Siberia is the vast region east of the Urals.

**Trans-Siberian Railway**
The world's longest railway line, running from Moscow to the Pacific port of Vladivostok and passing through Novosibirsk and Irkutsk. It skirts the southern end of Lake Baikal, while the later Baikal–Amur Mainline runs north of the lake.

**Gulags**
Soviet forced-labor camps, many of them in Siberia. The Kolyma region and its port of Magadan in the far northeast held some of the harshest camps.

**Jewish Autonomous Oblast and Birobidzhan**
A Russian region set up by Stalin in the 1930s along the Amur River as a homeland for Soviet Jews. Its capital, Birobidzhan, is the center of what is often called the world's only Jewish administrative division.

**Irkutsk**
A major city in southern Siberia on the Angara River, near the southwestern end of Lake Baikal. Like Novosibirsk, Siberia's largest city, it is a stop on the Trans-Siberian Railway.

**Kamchatka Peninsula and the Sea of Okhotsk**
A volcanic peninsula in the Russian Far East that encloses the Sea of Okhotsk on its east. It contains the Valley of Geysers, one of the world's largest geyser fields.

**Lena, Yenisei, Ob and Irtysh Rivers**
Siberia's great rivers, most of which flow north into the Arctic Ocean. The Lena empties into the Laptev Sea and the Yenisei into the Kara Sea. The Irtysh is the Ob's main tributary.

**Paleo-Siberian languages**
A grouping of unrelated or loosely related languages in northeastern Siberia, including Chukchi, Yukaghir (spoken in the Kolyma basin) and Nivkh, a language isolate of the Gilyak people. Ainu is sometimes linked to this grouping, and the Chukchi are among Native Americans' closest Old World relatives.

**Sakha Republic (Yakutia)**
The largest subnational division in the world, in northeastern Siberia, home to the Turkic-speaking Sakha (Yakut) people. Soviet underground nuclear explosions there have been linked to raised cancer rates.

**Yamal Peninsula**
A peninsula in northwestern Siberia, home to the reindeer-herding Nenets people, who live in conical tents called chum. Since 2014 several giant craters have appeared there, thought to come from methane gas bursting out of thawing permafrost.

**Siberian Traps**
A huge region of volcanic rock formed by enormous eruptions about 252 million years ago. These eruptions are considered the main cause of the Permian–Triassic extinction, the largest mass extinction in Earth's history.

**Dyatlov Pass incident**
The 1959 deaths of nine Soviet hikers on the slopes of Kholat Syakhl in the northern Ural Mountains, which inspired many conspiracy theories. A 2021 study using a simulation adapted from the snow-animation code of the film Frozen supported a slab avalanche as the cause.

**Nazino tragedy**
A 1933 disaster in which thousands of deportees were left on Nazino Island in the Ob River with almost no food, leading to mass death and cannibalism. It is the subject of the documentary Cannibal Island.

**Tuva and Buryatia**
Republics in southern Siberia. Tuva borders Mongolia and was historically claimed by the Republic of China (Taiwan), and Buryatia, with capital Ulan-Ude, is home to the Mongolic-speaking Buryat people.
